prose.detail:
The commodity page offers five commodities and eight species in total: Cow (0102) with Bison bison, Bos spp., Bos taurus and Bubalus bubalis; Horse (0101) with Equus caballus; Cat (01061900) with Felis catus; Dog (01061900) with Canis lupus familiaris; Fish (0301) with Salmo salar. The list is not filtered or paged, so that is the whole catalogue a user can reach. It is a hard-coded module — [[c1]] — and its own comment says the non-cow commodities carry "one representative species each". A user importing sheep, pigs, goats, poultry, rabbits, camels, parrots, reptiles, bees or ferrets has no option to choose.

DR1 carries twenty-one commodities — Bees, Camel, Cat, Cattle, Chicken, Dog, Duck, Ferret, Goat, Goose, Guinea fowl, Horse, Ornamental fish, Ostrich, Other live mammals, Parrot, Pig, Rabbit, Reptile, Sheep and Turkey — with their species beneath them ([[c2]]). Cattle alone carries eleven species against the frontend's four, Horse three against one, Ornamental fish three against one, and "Other live mammals" more than a hundred. Each commodity also carries the per-commodity rules that hang off it: which identifiers it needs, whether it asks for a package count, and whether it asks the unweaned question.

Widen the commodity catalogue to DR1's twenty-one commodities and their species. This replaces as well as adds: DR1 has no farmed-fish commodity at all, so the frontend's Fish (0301) with Salmo salar has no DR1 counterpart and gives way to Ornamental fish (030111) with Cichlidae, Cyprinidae and Poeciliidae. The catalogue is a local data module on both sides, so this is a data change rather than an integration, but every commodity carries rules with it, and in the frontend those rules are eight allow-lists keyed by commodity name in the same module — package count, passport, tattoo, ear tag, horse name, permanent address, unweaned animals and CPH, at [[c3]]. Each new commodity needs an entry in every list that applies to it, and three of those entries are why other parts of this comparison raised no finding of their own and deferred to this one. First, permanent address: DR1 requires a permanent address for Ferret as well as for cat and dog, so the permanent-address list has to gain Ferret when Ferret lands. Second, ear tag: DR1 gives Pig, Sheep and Goat an ear tag, where the frontend's ear-tag list is Cow alone. Third, CPH: DR1 decides the CPH question from the commodity code and asks it for every code except horses and the 01061900 group of cat, dog, ferret and other live mammals, so Pig (0103), Sheep, Goat and most of the new commodities all need a CPH number where the frontend's CPH list is Cow alone. Do not port DR1's per-commodity certification-purpose lists; they are unused data on the requirements side, where the certification question is fed by one flat sixteen-option list that does not vary by commodity. Confirm before starting that the notification payload mapping accepts the new commodity codes; if it does not, this becomes backend work first.

Every row on the frontend dashboard carries a Delete link ([[c1]]). It opens a page of its own headed "Delete this notification?" whose only body text is "This cannot be undone.", offering a red "Yes, delete notification" button and a "No, return to dashboard" button ([[c2]]). The action is not limited to drafts: [[c3]] admits draft, submitted and amending notifications alike, so a notification the authority has already received can be removed from the user's dashboard with one confirmation and no explanation of what that means. The frontend's empty dashboard says so itself: "You have not started any notifications in this session." ([[c1]], rendered at [[c2]]). The dashboard asks for a list of the journey ids this session happens to remember, not a list of the user's notifications: [[c3]] reads the ids out of the session store and passes them to the list query as a filter, and they live there for the life of the session ([[c4]]). Which notifications that actually produces depends on which store is behind it, and neither answer is the user's own. Against the stub, the filter is applied ([[c5]]), so a user who signs out, comes back tomorrow, or opens the service on a second device meets an empty dashboard whatever they created or submitted before — that is the captured behaviour. Against the real backend the filter is silently dropped: the list read sends only page, sort and reference number ([[c6]]), so the dashboard shows every notification the service holds, including other people's.

DR1 heads the list "My notifications" and shows four notifications belonging to the user, three of them submitted days earlier with an arrival date in the future and a status the authority has since set ([[c7]]). Two of the four read "Submitted action required", a state that can only be reached after the user has gone away and come back. DR1's status filter offers Approved, Rejected and Complete on the same terms, so the list is required to survive the session that created it.

The dashboard has to list the notifications belonging to the signed-in user or their organisation — not the ones this browser session happens to remember, and not everything the service holds. That means the list read stops filtering on session-held journey ids and asks the backend for the caller's notifications instead, which needs the list endpoint to support an owner-scoped query and the records to carry an owner. Do this before the status work and the filter work: filtering a session's handful of drafts by status or arrival date has little to filter. The real adapter dropping the session filter is a separate defect from the parity gap and wants raising on its own, but the fix here supersedes it — an owner-scoped read is what both need.

The user picks one of five reasons on its own page and presses Save and continue, and the follow-up questions arrive as separate pages afterwards, one field per page. Internal market leads to a Purpose in the internal market page; Transhipment or onward travel leads to a Destination country page; Transit leads to a Port of exit page and then a Destination country page; Temporary admission horses leads to an Exit date page and then a Port of exit page; Re-entry leads straight on. The five pages are declared as five entries in one flow section in [[c1]], and which of them a user meets is decided by the four gates in [[c2]].

DR1 asks all of it on /reason-for-import. The four gates already encode exactly the right conditions and do not change — this is a change of where the questions are rendered and validated, not of when they apply. The work is: render the purpose radios, destination country, port of exit and exit date as conditional HTML on the reason page in the order DR1 shows them (transit: port of exit above destination country; temporary admission: exit date above port of exit); validate reason and the revealed field in one pass and return errors against the revealed control; fold the hub's "Exit details" row into "Main reason for importing" so the two rows become one, which also retires the "Cannot start yet" state that row is the only user of; and adopt DR1's page heading, which is a separate finding because it can be done on its own. Do this before the smaller findings that edit those pages' controls, or expect to move that work twice.

prose.detail:
Every page in the journey renders its content in a two-thirds column, so nothing a user meets is ever wider than about 630 pixels of a 960-pixel container. The width is decided once, for the whole service, by the shared page base (`[[c1]]`), which hard-codes the narrow surface and gives no page a way to ask for anything else; the shared layout then prints it (`[[c2]]`). The frontend already knows the wide surface exists — `[[c3]]` names both, `form` and `display` — and exactly one page uses it: the notification list, which passes `display` from its own controller (`[[c4]]`). Everything else inherits the narrow one, whatever it holds. The effect is worst where the content is tabular: the check-your-answers summary cards, the task list, the document table, the address picker and the animal identification cards all render at the width of a paragraph, so values wrap onto three and four lines and the page grows correspondingly long.

DR1 decides width per page and per element rather than once for the service. Its prose and its form fields are held to about 630 pixels wherever they appear, the same as the frontend, but anything tabular is given the whole 960-pixel container. Fifteen of the 42 DR1 screens render content wider than the frontend can: the two review states (`[[c5]]`), the notification hub, all seven upload-documents states, the transporter directory, the commodity details table, the animal identification cards, the address select list and the permanent address cards. On several of those the same page does both — the upload-documents intro wraps at 630 and the File upload card beneath it runs the full 960.

Let a page choose its content surface, and choose the wide one where DR1 does. The mechanism is already built and already proven on one page, so the work is to stop the shared base hard-coding `SURFACES.form` — take the surface as an option defaulting to `form` — and then pass `display` from the controllers of the pages DR1 renders wide: check your answers, the task list, documents, the address pickers, animal identification, commodity details and the transporter list. Nothing else changes: no copy, no fields, no routes, and the narrow surface stays the default so any page not named keeps the width it has today. Worth doing as one change rather than page by page, because the reason it is wrong everywhere is that it is decided in one place.

The list the user is choosing from is thirty-one countries long, so more than twelve is reachable.

DR1 states no ceiling anywhere on the page — its hint is "Enter each country that the consignment will travel through" — and its handling of the answer normalises and stores whatever was added without counting it ([[c4]]).

Remove the cap and the hint that announces it. If a limit is genuinely wanted, it needs to be stated in DR1 first, because the number twelve appears nowhere in the signed-off design. This is one of two rules the frontend puts on this field that DR1 does not; the other is that it may not be empty.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a stated or enforced maximum number of transit countries in DR1 — its transit-country handling stores the normalised list without any length check.

prose.detail:
Under the label "Select all countries the consignment will travel through" the page renders every country as a checkbox in one alphabetical column, thirty-one of them from Austria to Switzerland, and the user scrolls and ticks ([[c1]]). What is stored is a set, deduplicated and unordered ([[c2]]). There is no search, nothing shows back which countries have been chosen apart from the ticks themselves, and there is nothing to remove — a user un-ticks. Nothing anywhere records that the consignment passes through France before Belgium.

The page asks "Enter a country", hinted "Enter each country that the consignment will travel through", over a single search box placeholdered "Search for a country" ([[c3]]). Each country the user picks is appended to a list below headed "Country", one row each, with a "Remove" link on the right. The list keeps the order they were added in, and the review page prints them in that order.

Replace the checkbox list with a country search that appends to a growing, removable list, and store the answer as an ordered sequence rather than a set. This changes what the answer means as well as how it is collected, so the stored shape and anything that reads it — the hub, the review page, the submitted payload — has to accept an ordered list. It travels with the two findings about the rules the frontend puts on this field, since all three change the same control.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a search input or a remove control on fe-transit-countries — the captured DOM for that screen is one checkbox group and the Save buttons.

prose.detail:
The transited-countries obligation is gated on the means of transport being rail or road, and where it applies its status is mandatory ([[c1]]). Submitting the page with nothing ticked is rejected with "Select at least one country the consignment will travel through" ([[c2]]). A consignment that crosses no third country — a lorry from the Republic of Ireland, say — has no honest answer to give, and the hub cannot be completed without one.

DR1 puts the page in the journey under the same condition, when the means of transport is Railway or Road Vehicle, and then lets it be left empty: the handler for the page saves whatever was submitted and redirects onward without validating anything, so pressing Save and continue with no country added takes the user to the next page ([[c3]]). Submission is not blocked either — the review card for transit countries is built with its error state permanently off, under the line "Transit countries are optional for submission" ([[c4]]). DR1 does not call an empty answer finished, though: its hub row for Transit countries reads "To do" until at least one country has been added ([[c5]]). The captured empty state shows Save and continue live with no country in the list.

Drop the at-least-one rule so the page can be saved and left with nothing chosen, and let a rail or road notification reach submission with no transit countries recorded. The gate itself — rail or road only — already matches DR1 and does not change, and neither does the hub: both sides leave the row outstanding while the list is empty, so it is the page and the submission that differ, not the task list. This should land with the change to the control, since both alter the same field. Neither side's captured screen shows the state after pressing Save and continue with nothing chosen, so the claim rests on reading the frontend's validator and DR1's route handler; photographing both sides at that moment would put it beyond argument.

FALSIFIED BY: Submitting fe-transit-countries with no country ticked and being taken onward — the controller returns 400 with the "Select at least one country" error whenever the selection is empty, on either button, because it validates before it branches on the exit action.

The checkboxes are drawn from the frontend's origin-country list ([[c1]]). Thirty-one entries: the twenty-seven EU member states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. No overseas territory or Crown Dependency appears, and no country outside the EU and EFTA does either. Three labels differ from DR1's for the same place — "Czechia", "Ireland" and "Netherlands (the)".

The search is fed a forty-one entry list ([[c2]]). It holds the twenty-seven EU member states, eleven EU outermost regions and overseas entities — Azores, Canary Islands, Ceuta, French Guiana, Guadeloupe, Madeira, Martinique, Mayotte, Melilla, Réunion, Saint Martin — and three Crown Dependencies, Guernsey, Isle of Man and Jersey. Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland are absent. The United Kingdom is absent too, matching the page's own line "This does not include the United Kingdom".

Settle which list is right before changing either side, because taking DR1 literally would both add and remove countries and each direction looks wrong on its face. DR1's own copy defines these as "countries between the country of origin and the destination country" — a consignment does not travel through Réunion, Mayotte, Martinique or French Guiana on its way to Great Britain, so DR1's data contradicts DR1's sentence; and dropping Switzerland and Norway would stop a user recording the most ordinary road route into GB from southern Europe. What settles it is the authoritative list of countries a consignment may be recorded as transiting — the same list the backend validates the submitted notification against — and a decision on whether one shared country list can serve both "where is this party's address" and "where does the consignment pass through", which is what put the territories in DR1's transit list in the first place. On the frontend the two questions already share one list too, so the change is not local to this page.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding Norway, Switzerland, Iceland or Liechtenstein in DR1's transit-country data, or finding any of the eleven overseas territories in the frontend's — the two datasets are captured in full in the rendered DOM for each screen and neither overlaps the other on those entries.

prose.detail:
Each transporter is one radio whose label is the name and whose hint is the address and approval number run together — "43 East Hague Extension, …, Switzerland — approval number ES-T2-45001294" ([[c1]]). There is no type, no approval status and no way to see anything more about a transporter before choosing it. A user picking between two similar names has only the address to go on.

The transporters are a table with a header row and six columns — Name, Address, Approval number, Type, Status and a per-row link ([[c2]]). Type reads "Commercial" or "Private". Status is a coloured tag, "Approved" or "New". The last column is a "View details" link to that transporter's own page.

Render the transporter list as a table with the DR1 columns rather than as radio hints: add Type, add the approval-status tag, and add a per-row link to the transporter's details. The status tag needs a source of truth for whether a transporter is approved or newly added, which the frontend's fixed record list does not carry today ([[c3]]), so that field has to be added to whatever supplies the list. Do it with the search field, which changes the same list.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a status, type or details link anywhere on fe-transporter-commercial — the captured DOM for that screen has one fieldset containing two radios and their hints, and no table element at all.

prose.detail:
The transporter section opens with "What type of transporter will move the animals?" and two radios — Commercial, hinted "A business approved to transport animals — you will choose one from a list", and Private, hinted "You or another individual moving the animals — you will give their address" ([[c1]]). The answer routes the user to one of two pages that offer no way back to the other and no way to add anything: a commercial-only pick list, or an empty private-transporter form ([[c2]] makes the two mutually exclusive, purging the commercial answer when the type flips to Private and the reverse). A private transporter the user has used before must be typed in again, and a commercial one can never be typed in at all.

The section opens on the directory itself — "Transporter details", then "Select a transporter" over one table that mixes Commercial and Private rows and marks which is which in a Type column ([[c3]]). The user picks a row. The type question exists only behind the "Add a transporter" button, where its heading is "Choose a transporter type" under the caption "Add a new transporter", it is preceded by the warning "Before you add this transporter, please ensure you have already searched for it first", it lists Private transporter before Commercial, and its Commercial option carries an entirely different meaning: "This can only be a commercial transporter from Northern Ireland".

Move the transporter section's entry from the type question to the directory, and make the directory hold private transporters as well as commercial ones. The type question becomes a step inside the add journey, reworded to DR1's heading and hints and with Private listed first. Everything a user does today stays reachable — choosing from the commercial list becomes choosing a Commercial row, and entering a private transporter becomes adding one — but both now start from the list. Do this before the add-a-commercial-transporter finding, which hangs off the same button.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding a private transporter listed anywhere on fe-transporter-commercial, or a route that reaches the frontend's transporter list without first answering the type question — the transporters-select page is reached only from the type page and its list is the fixed commercial record set.
